name: Radon therapy

card.summary: Radon therapy is the deliberate exposure to low levels of radon in spa baths, drinking water or mine galleries, used by practitioners for joint and inflammatory conditions and promoted at spas as invigorating.
card.aka: Radon spa; radon balneotherapy; radon health mine
card.note: Radon is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen; lung cancer is the established harm.

quick.overview:
Radon therapy means spending time in radon-bearing water, air or mine tunnels, as offered at spa sites in Central Europe, Japan and the US. Practitioners and visitors cite relief of arthritis and other joint pain, and some spas promote an energizing effect.

For looks, the connection is claimed and indirect: any benefit would come through joint comfort and general well-being. Reviews describe benefits reported in rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and osteoarthritis, with variable study quality, and describe radon as a major cause of lung cancer.
quick.how: Treatment forms include warm radon baths, breathing air in radon galleries such as Bad Gastein's, and drinking radon water. Courses are run at established spas, often within a spa-medicine setting and combined with heat.
quick.risks: The WHO classifies radon as a Group 1 carcinogen and the second leading cause of lung cancer worldwide. Reviews note that heat and other spa elements confound the clinical results and that regulatory restrictions exist.

lead: Radon therapy is the intentional use of low-dose radon exposure, delivered as baths, inhalation in galleries or mines, or drinking water, at spas and health mines. Radioactive baths have been used at Jáchymov (Czech Republic) since 1906, and inhalation therapy is offered at Bad Gastein in Austria, Boulder and Basin in Montana, and other sites [1][5].

Visitors and spa operators describe pain relief in arthritis and a general invigorating effect. For someone interested in appearance, the link is claimed: better joint comfort and well-being could support activity and training, but radon therapy is not a treatment for any facial or body-composition feature.

Reviews of the area describe a mix of therapeutic and risk findings. Radon therapy has been investigated mainly for rheumatic and musculoskeletal disorders, while radon exposure itself is established as a cause of lung cancer [2][3][4].

chain: Claimed reduction of joint pain and inflammation
angle.text: Spas promote radon sessions for pain relief and an energizing effect. Any link to appearance runs through comfort and activity, not a direct cosmetic action.

infobox: Bad Gastein, Jáchymov, Misasa, Boulder MT

paras: Radon therapy delivers radon through bathing in radon water, inhaling radon-rich air in galleries or mines, or drinking radon water. Sites include the Gasteiner Heilstollen in Bad Gastein, Misasa in Japan, Bad Brambach in Germany, Kowary in Poland and Montana health mines [5].

The most prominent claim is relief from arthritis symptoms, with spas also promoting a low-dose energizing effect [5]. Reviews describe proposed mechanisms including modulation of oxidative stress, immune signalling and inflammatory cytokines [3][2].

A meta-analysis of controlled trials examined the effect of radon therapy on pain in rheumatic diseases [4]. A 2026 narrative review reported benefits in pain, function and quality of life in rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and osteoarthritis, while noting heterogeneity in protocols and study quality and confounding by heat and carbon dioxide [3]. A 2026 review states the strength of clinical evidence varies by indication, with neurological and cancer applications largely experimental [2].

Radon is a WHO Group 1 carcinogen, the second leading cause of lung cancer worldwide, and lung cancer is the only outcome firmly established as caused by radon [2]. Wikipedia notes the WHO home reference level of 100 Bq/m3 and that intentional exposure is controversial [5]. Reviews describe the biological effects of chronic exposure and therapeutic exposure as still under investigation [1].

timeline.event: Radioactive baths in use at Jáchymov [5].
